summary: Guidelines for K-12 schools planning telecommunications. It introduces the role of the Internet in education and gives a recommended technical direction for building a campus data network. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A how-to guide for schools that want to connect their classrooms to the internet.

subtitle: A 1994 planning guide for connecting schools, districts and counties to the Internet with TCP/IP.

tldr.problem: K-12 schools wanted to use data communications, but state plans gave no specific technical direction and schools rarely had staff for telecommunications planning.
tldr.mechanism: The guide recommends TCP/IP and a hierarchy: a LAN in each school with a server and router, a link to the district office, and a connection from the district (or county) to an Internet service provider, plus central network operations and support.
tldr.outcome: It gives a practical model and numbers for wiring, capacity and staffing so schools of any size can start now, without building a new statewide backbone.

facts.label: Bandwidth use target
facts.value: no more than 10% on a typical work day

today: RFC 1709 is an Informational RFC from November 1994 (FYI 26), and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its figures and technology choices reflect 1994 practice, such as LocalTalk, ISDN and Frame Relay circuits.

sections.title: Why Schools Needed Guidance
sections.content: State plans recommended voice, video and data networks for learning and administration, but gave no specific technical direction. Early Internet institutions had dedicated technical staff, which the K-12 community traditionally lacked. This document is meant to bridge that gap with a recommended technical direction, an introduction to the Internet's role in K-12 education and guidelines for building a campus data network with Internet connections.
sections.eli5: Schools wanted computers talking to each other but did not have network experts, so this guide explains what to do.

sections.title: Why Use TCP/IP
sections.content:
The guide cites a 1993 Bank Street College of Education survey of 550 educators who actively use telecommunications. E-mail was the most common use: 91 percent for professional activities and 79 percent for student activities, ahead of news or bulletin boards (63 and 50).

It argues that the same TCP/IP protocols used on the Internet can build campus-wide networks, and lists the benefits as ubiquity, applications, flexibility, simplicity, capacity, coexistence with other networking architectures, multimedia support, compatibility and the planned NREN. Coexistence matters because offices may already run AppleTalk, Novell NetWare, LANManager or SNA.
sections.eli5: TCP/IP is a language almost every computer already speaks, so using it means all the school's computers can talk to each other and to the world.

sections.title: The Four-Step Network Model
sections.content:
The basic model is simple: create a LAN in each school building or cluster, provide at least one network server for it, interconnect it with the district offices (where a similar LAN and central resources should exist), and connect the district offices to the nearest Internet service provider, possibly through the county office of education. Using existing providers avoids the major expense of new statewide backbones.

The guide sets design criteria: reusable wiring (wiring is typically 20 to 40% of the cost of individual network hookups), integrating existing computers, well-placed servers, and links that are cost effective. Reliability should be well over 99.7%, and no more than 10% of bandwidth should be used during a typical work day.

Primary technical support should come from the district or county offices at first, with local schools taking on more as expertise grows.
sections.eli5: Each school gets its own little network. The schools link to the district office, and the district links to the Internet company.

sections.title: Building the School LAN and Links
sections.content:
Ethernet is recommended for all computer connections where possible and for the school backbone, since it is roughly 20 to 40 times faster than LocalTalk. IEEE 802.5 Token Ring is not recommended for new installations. Premise wiring should be a star of category 5 unshielded twisted pair, with 4 pair cable recommended, running to a hub site that must be within 300 feet of any connection. As many as 250 computers can attach to one ethernet segment, but 100-125 is the planning figure.

Each school should have a local network server, typically 1-4 gigabytes of disk, and a network router. Schools connect individually to the district router in a star. Dedicated circuits are strongly recommended over dial-up or switched services. The options listed range from a 20 kilobit per second voice grade line, ADN-56, ISDN and low power radio to Frame Relay and DS1 at 1.5 megabits per second. For Frame Relay, the combined capacity of school links should not exceed the capacity into the district office by more than a factor of 3.
sections.eli5: Run a cable from every room to a closet, use the fast kind of network, put a helper computer in the school, and pay for a line that is always on.

sections.title: Management, DNS and Support
sections.content:
The district office is the focal point. It manages DNS service for its schools, assigns IP addresses and keeps node names. The district server should initially hold the DNS database, with secondary service on larger school servers later. Monitoring with SNMP serves three purposes: watching network health, collecting statistics, and faster problem resolution.

Support is organised around a Network Operations Center (NOC), which installs and monitors the network, and a Network Information Center (NIC), which provides help desk, training and information services. Every organisation using e-mail should have a Postmaster and a mailbox named postmaster. The guide notes that these duties can be shared by existing staff.
sections.eli5: Someone has to watch the network, answer questions and keep a list of names and addresses, just like a school office does for phones.

sections.title: Existing Networks
sections.content: Older school LANs that can carry Internet protocols may be integrated and replaced later as funding permits. Token Ring can be linked in using routers that support it, and a Novell ethernet LAN can carry Internet and Novell protocols at the same time. Using a server as a 'network application gateway' is strongly discouraged, because each computer should support Internet protocols directly. Older LAN technologies should not be expanded and should be phased out as funding permits.
sections.eli5: Old school networks can be plugged into the new one for now, but the plan is to replace them over time.
